title: Start here
goals: Know what you will be able to do at the end, and how this course is built to get you there.

q: Before anything else, a guess. The HP drum level on the DCS slowly climbs while feedwater flow reads higher than steam flow. What is the most likely first thing you should do?

why: Tripping is for the protection limits (+550 mm on the HP drum). A slowly rising level is first a control problem. Killing the unit for it costs a start and risks a thermal shock.

text: Check the level against the local gauge and check drum and feedwater pressures, then take the feed control to manual if the automatic control is wrong.
why: That is the manual's sequence for high level (§7.4.1): confirm the reading is real, then control the feed. You will learn the numbers and the reasoning in Modules 2, 4 and 10.

text: Open every blowdown valve fully to drop the level fast.
why: Emergency discharge and continuous blowdown do help (and open automatically at +450 mm), but blowing down hard without knowing whether the reading is real can drop you into a low-level trip.

label: Why · general boiler practice, not stated in the manual

p: "Natural circulation" means no pump drives water through the evaporator. The flow comes only from the density difference between cold water in the downcomers and the lighter steam-water mixture in the hot tubes. If drum level falls too far, the downcomers stop being fed, circulation weakens and evaporator tubes can run dry and overheat. If level rises too far, water is carried into the superheater and on towards the turbine. Almost every limit in Module 2 protects one of those two failures.

label: Why

p: The HP drum wall is 125 mm thick. Thick steel heats from the inside first, so the inner surface expands before the outer one. Heat it too fast and the stress cracks it over many cycles. That single fact explains the heating-rate limits and the 40 °C top-to-bottom limit you will meet in Module 7.

small: §1.1.1, §1.1.6–1.1.8, §1.1.5 (water volumes: LP drum 146 m³, HP drum 45 m³, total system 580 m³).

case: Why does the manual allow the superheater header to heat at 25 °C/min during a cold start, but the HP drum only 5 °C/min?
steps: Look at what is different between the parts
The HP drum wall is 125 mm thick. Headers and tubes are much thinner.
Think about how thick steel heats
Heat enters at the inside surface. Across a thick wall, the inside gets hot long before the outside, so the inside tries to expand while the outside holds it back.
Link it to damage
That difference creates thermal stress. The thicker the wall, the bigger the temperature difference for the same heating rate, and the bigger the stress.
Conclusion
The thickest part gets the slowest rate (drum under 5 °C/min), thinner parts get more (SH header under 25, others under 30 °C/min). Same logic gives the 40 °C top-to-bottom drum limit.

q: Where do the HP and IP feed pumps take their suction from?

why: The condensate pumps take from the hotwell. The HP and IP feed pumps are after the LP drum.
Yes. Before starting either feed pump the manual checks LP drum level is normal (§2.2.4), because a low LP drum starves them.
The IP drum is fed by the IP feed pump. It is not a suction source.

q: Which drum has the thickest wall, and what does that mean for operation?

text: LP, because it is the largest drum, so it needs the slowest filling.
why: The LP drum is the largest (3.5 m × 16.5 m) but its wall is only 30 mm because it runs at 0.67 MPa.

text: HP, 125 mm, so it limits how fast the unit can heat up and cool down.
why: Correct. The 125 mm HP drum sets the 5 °C/min drum heating limit and the 40 °C top-to-bottom limit.

text: IP, 46 mm, because it has the highest design temperature.
why: IP is 46 mm. The HP drum is far thicker because it holds 12.44 MPa.

q: The HP drum level drops very low while the unit is at load. What is the physical danger to the evaporator?

text: The downcomers are no longer fed properly, circulation weakens and evaporator tubes can overheat.
why: Yes. With natural circulation, water supply to the tubes depends on the drum level. That is why the low-level trip exists.

text: Steam pressure rises and lifts the safety valves.
why: Low level does not by itself raise pressure. The risk is to the tubes that lose their water.

text: Water is carried over into the superheater.
why: Carry-over is the danger of HIGH level, not low.

q: Gas turbine exhaust is about 581 °C. Which surfaces meet it first?

text: The condensate heater and LP economizer.
why: These are at the cold end, just before the stack. They use the last low-temperature heat.
Yes. They need the highest steam temperature (about 560 °C), so they sit where the gas is hottest.
IP sections sit in the middle of the gas path, after the HP sections.

case: At 85% load the HP drum level reads +430 mm and is rising slowly. Feedwater flow is 12 t/h above steam flow. Drum and feed pressures are steady. What do you conclude and do?
steps: Place it on the ladder
+430 is above the high alarm (+400) and below the point where the emergency discharge valve opens (+450). Trip is +550. You have about 120 mm before a trip.
Is the reading real?
Pressures are steady, so this is not swell from a pressure drop. Compare with the local gauge. Feedwater exceeding steam flow agrees with a real rise, so the level is probably real.
Find the cause
More water in than steam out, with no load change, points at the feed control: the automatic control or the valve is feeding too much (§7.4.1 reasons 1–3).
Act

Take feed control to manual and reduce the valve opening. If flow does not respond, close the manual valve before the control valve locally and feed through the bypass. Confirm the EDV and continuous blowdown open at +450. Call maintenance. Watch superheater outlet temperature for any sudden drop (sign of carry-over).

why: Correct. IP: low alarm −300, trip −350. This is where you act at once to restore feed.
The IP low trip is −350. −320 is just above it.

q: Which drum level setting opens the HP emergency discharge valve?

why: +400 is the first high alarm only.
Yes. +450 gives a high alarm and opens the emergency discharge valve.
+550 is the HRSG trip.

why: Right. LP: alarm −1300, low-low −1350, trip −1400. The HP and IP feed pumps take suction from this drum.
LP trip is −1400.

The manual asks for more than normal.
Yes. As the water cools and bubbles collapse, the level shrinks. Starting at NWL+100 keeps the tubes covered.

q: Guess: HP drum level on the DCS has read exactly −50 mm for 40 minutes while load went from 60% to 90%. Feed and steam flow rose together. What is the best explanation?

Drum level is judged by the

case: Night shift. The HP drum level on the DCS falls from −60 to −190 mm over 10 minutes. Load is steady. Feedwater flow and steam flow are both 278 t/h. Drum pressure is steady. What is going on?
steps: Mass balance
Feed equals steam and load is steady, so the amount of water in the drum should not be changing. The mass balance says the level is steady.
Pressure
No pressure change, so this is not swell or shrink.
Therefore
The instrument is the prime suspect, not the process. A water-side leak or blockage on the level measurement reads low.
Act

Compare with both local gauges. If they read normal, do not add feed to "correct" the DCS number, because you would overfill the drum. Put feed control on a trusted signal or manual, flush or repair the faulty gauge, and record it.

Swinging, not rising steadily. That is not the signature of full water.

Temperature and chemistry
Falling steam temperature plus rising salt in steam means water is being carried over with the steam.
Diagnosis
Foaming (§7.4.3): poor boiler water or continuous blowdown too small.
Action
